name: Liberia Kpelle
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Welmers 1962, The phonology of Kpelle, Journal of African Languages 1:69-93; not found online

new_statements.quote: [p. 51] Words with high, high-low, and low tone patterns have stress on the initial syllable. Mid-high-low have stress on the second vowel, since this stress is automatic and does not differentiate one word from another (as English stress does in 'progress' as a noun and 'progress' as a verb). [p. 190] While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is generally distinctive. In Kpelle, it falls on the first high-toned syllable in the word, or if the word has no high tones, it falls on the first syllable. Stress is acoustically marked by an increase in the loudness of the syllable and is often accompanied by a slight increase in the length of the syllable.
new_statements.citation: Thach, Sharon V. with David J. Dwyer. 1981. Kpelle: A Reference Handbook of Phonetics, Grammar, Lexicon and Learning Procedures. East Lansing: African Studies Center, Michigan State University, for the US Peace Corps (ERIC ED217690).
new_statements.locator: p. 51, §IV.B.3 'Tones, Stress, Intonation', item c (pdf page 53); and p. 190, Appendix E 'Mande Suprasegmentals', §2 'Stress' (pdf page 190)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kpelle is a three-level tone language (high, mid, low) in which stress is automatic and non-contrastive, predictable from the word's tone pattern: it falls on the first high-toned syllable of the word; in words with no high tone (low-throughout words per p. 51; 'no high tones' per p. 190) it falls on the first syllable. Under the five-pattern analysis of p. 51 this puts stress on the initial syllable for H, HL and L words and on the second vowel for the mid-high-low pattern. Correlates: loudness plus slight lengthening. Welmers 1962: 86 (as digested by the Stanford Phonology Archive 1979) says the same in toneme terms: stress is non-phonemic, conditioned by tone, always with the first high or low tone of the word and never with mid.
new_statements.exceptions: Mid-high-low words stress the second vowel (p. 51). The two pages disagree on all-mid words: p. 190 gives first syllable when there is no high tone, whereas Welmers 1962: 86 (via SPA 1979) says stress never occurs with mid tone. In the Gbarnga area /k/, /g/ and especially /ɣ/ are not pronounced in an unstressed syllable between two front vowels (p. 51). Sinclair 1968: xxiv (pedagogical) instead says syllables receive equal stress with slight extra stress on a falling-tone syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; p. 51e states the tone patterns 'apply to words without prefixes or suffixes', affixes carrying their own tone patterns. Stress is explicitly automatic and non-distinctive; the language is tonal.
new_statements.identity_note: Thach & Dwyer 1981 describes Liberian Kpelle as taught to Peace Corps volunteers (Totota Lutheran orthography, Bong County; dialect notes for Gbarnga, Totota, Jorquellie), i.e. libe1247. The Konoshenko 2017 Jazyki mira chapter already on file under guin1254 states that phonological stress is absent, but explicitly for central Guinean Kpelle (Hɔŋkwele variety, Nzérékoré) = guin1254, a different glottocode; do not transfer that statement to libe1247. Welmers 1962 (Liberian Kpelle, SPA digest p. 86) agrees with the handbook that stress is non-phonemic and tone-conditioned.

sources.note: p. 51 (Short Summary Reference Grammar, B.3 'Tones, Stress, Intonation'): words with high, high-low and low tone patterns are stressed on the initial syllable, mid-high-low words on the second vowel; stress is automatic and non-distinctive; in the Gbarnga area /k/, /g/, /ɣ/ drop in an unstressed syllable between front vowels. p. 190 (Appendix E 'Mande Suprasegmentals', 2 'Stress'): stress non-contrastive; in Kpelle it falls on the first high-toned syllable, or on the first syllable if the word has no high tones; marked by loudness and slight lengthening.

sources.note: Second-hand digest of Welmers 1962: 'STRESS: "Stress...is non-phonemic...conditioned by tone." Stress always occurs with the first /high/, or /low/, tone of a word. Stress never occurs with /mid/ tone. (p. 86)' — locates Welmers's stress statement at JAL 1:86.

sources.note: Pedagogical course; p. xxiv ('Tone'): 'In these words, each syllable receives equal stress. There is, however, a slight additional stress given to the syllable which takes a "falling" tone.' Unit I Lesson 1: words written with a falling-tone mark on the last syllable 'receive slight stress on that syllable'.
